questions.a: In order from earliest to latest.

questions.q: What goes in a fact box?
questions.a: An interesting fact or a quote by the person.

days.guide: Rehearse a 1-minute first-person speech ('I am Sally Ride…'), speaking audibly in complete sentences.

questions.q: Start a living museum speech as Abraham Lincoln.
questions.a: Example: I am Abraham Lincoln. I was the 16th President of the United States.

questions.q: Why speak in first person?
questions.a: Because you are pretending to be the person.

days.guide: Present the living museum to family. Give the unit test on a new biography.

questions.q: What is the author's purpose of a biography?
questions.a: To inform readers about a real person's life.

questions.q: What is the main topic of a biography?
questions.a: The person whose life it tells.

weeks.assessment_key: Research rubric (3 = proficient): 3 paragraphs (early life, big work, why we remember them) with accurate facts in own words; concluding sentence; poster with portrait, 5-event timeline in order, and a quote/fact box; speech in first person, audible, complete sentences. Unit test on the new biography: events sequenced correctly; main topic named; author's purpose = to inform about a real person's life.

weeks.prep: Get Volcanoes (Franklyn M. Branley, Let's-Read-and-Find-Out) and read it first. Gather clay (or play dough) around a small bottle, baking soda, vinegar, dish soap, red food coloring, and a tray. Print an earthquake passage and homophone pairs.
misconceptions: Thinking magma and lava are different materials. Both are melted rock — magma is underground; lava is magma that has come out.
Mixing up homophones (there/their). Their = belongs to them; there = a place.

days.guide: Read Volcanoes and study the diagram; label magma, crater, lava. Teach to/two/too and there/their.

questions.q: What is magma?
questions.a: Hot melted rock deep underground.

questions.q: What is lava?
questions.a: Magma that comes out of a volcano onto the surface.

days.guide: Find the point 'Volcanoes can build new land' and list the author's reasons. Write 'The author says ___ because ___.'

questions.q: What reasons support 'volcanoes can build new land'?
questions.a: The Hawaiian Islands were made by volcanoes, and the island of Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland.

questions.q: Complete: The author says volcanoes build land because ___.
questions.a: lava cools and hardens into new rock, piling up into islands.

days.guide: Build a clay volcano and erupt it with baking soda and vinegar. Write 3 steps. Teach see/sea and right/write.

questions.q: Is the model eruption a real volcano?
questions.a: No — it is a chemical reaction making foam; a real eruption is melted rock from underground.

questions.q: Use 'sea' in a sentence.
questions.a: Example: Surtsey rose out of the sea.

days.guide: Read an earthquake passage; identify one point and two reasons. Use context to define 'fault' and 'plates.'

questions.q: What are plates?
questions.a: Giant pieces of Earth's crust that slowly move.

questions.q: What is a fault?
questions.a: A crack in Earth's crust where plates move past each other and earthquakes can happen.

days.guide: Complete a points-and-reasons organizer on a new passage and take the homophone quiz.

questions.q: Fix: 'Their are two volcanoes.'
questions.a: There are two volcanoes.

questions.q: Choose: I like to ___ (write/right) stories.
questions.a: write.

weeks.assessment_key: Point-and-reasons organizer: proficient states the author's point and 2 reasons from the passage (e.g., 'Volcanoes can build new land' — reasons: the Hawaiian Islands were built by volcanoes; the island of Surtsey rose out of the sea near Iceland in 1963). Homophone quiz (12): to/two/too, there/their, see/sea, right/write, know/no, hear/here — each used correctly in a sentence. Eruption steps: 1) put baking soda in the volcano 2) poured in vinegar 3) bubbly foam flowed out like lava.

weeks.prep: Get How Mountains Are Made (Kathleen Weidner Zoehfeld) and a second mountain text, plus a children's dictionary. Prepare 10 science words to alphabetize and two short rock passages for Friday.
misconceptions: Alphabetizing only by the first letter. When first letters match, look at the second letter (magma, mountain).
Comparing texts by listing only one text's facts. Use 'Both…' and 'Only…' sentence frames.

days.guide: Read How Mountains Are Made and list 4 important points about how mountains form. Use headings to find facts.

questions.q: Name one way mountains form.
questions.a: Plates of Earth's crust push together and fold or lift up the land (others: volcanoes, blocks lifted along faults).

questions.q: What wears mountains down over time?
questions.a: Wind, water, and ice (erosion).

days.guide: Read a second mountain text, list its points, and star the points that match.

questions.q: Why star matching points?
questions.a: To show which ideas both texts agree on.

questions.q: How do volcanoes make mountains?
questions.a: Lava erupts, cools, and piles up into a mountain.

days.guide: Complete the two-text chart and write 3 compound sentences comparing the texts.

questions.q: Complete: Both texts say ___, but only the second ___.
questions.a: Example: Both texts say plates push mountains up, but only the second tells about volcanoes.

questions.q: Which joining word shows a difference?
questions.a: but.

days.guide: Alphabetize 10 science words to the second letter and use guide words to look them up.

questions.q: Alphabetize: mountain, magma, lava.
questions.a: lava, magma, mountain.

questions.q: What are guide words?
questions.a: The words at the top of a dictionary page showing the first and last words on that page.

days.guide: Compare two rock passages in a chart, take an ABC-order quiz, and do a dictionary look-up.

questions.q: Would 'pebble' be on a page with guide words 'peach–pencil'?
questions.a: Yes — 'peb' comes after 'pea' and before 'pen.'

questions.q: Alphabetize: rock, river, rain.
questions.a: rain, river, rock.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-text chart: points that both texts share are starred; 3 compound sentences comparing (e.g., 'Both texts say plates push up mountains, but only the second explains erosion'). ABC-order quiz (suggested): crater, earth, fault, lava, magma, mountain, plate, rock, slope, volcano. Dictionary check: child uses guide words to find a word and copies its definition correctly.

weeks.prep: Gather a seed packet, a simple trail-mix recipe and ingredients (e.g., cereal, raisins, pretzels; check allergies), measuring cups, and paper. Make a list of 12 multisyllable science words (ingredient, measure, sprinkle, minute, seedling, gather, together, important, number, finally, carefully, container).
misconceptions: Skipping steps that seem obvious. Have someone follow the directions exactly to find missing steps.
Steps without numbers or time-order words. Number each step and start with first, next, then, last.

days.guide: Read steps on a seed packet and a recipe. Discuss why order matters and what happens if a step is skipped.

questions.q: What could happen if you skip 'water the seeds'?
questions.a: The seeds might not sprout.

questions.q: Why are steps numbered?
questions.a: To show the order to follow.

days.guide: Make trail mix following written steps, then rewrite the steps in your own words with numbers and time-order words.

questions.q: Write step 1 for trail mix.
questions.a: Example: First, pour one cup of cereal into a bowl.

questions.q: Split 'ingredient' into syllables.
questions.a: in-gre-di-ent.

days.guide: Choose something you know how to do and list the materials and steps.

questions.q: List steps for making a sandwich.
questions.a: Example: 1) Get two slices of bread. 2) Spread peanut butter. 3) Put the slices together. 4) Cut it in half.

questions.q: What goes in a materials list?
questions.a: Everything you need to do the task.

days.guide: Draft the how-to with introduction, numbered steps, and closing. A family member follows it exactly and notes missing steps.

questions.q: Why have someone follow your steps exactly?
questions.a: To find steps that are missing or unclear.

questions.q: Write a closing for a sandwich how-to.
questions.a: Example: Now enjoy your tasty sandwich!

days.guide: Revise after testing, add diagrams, and publish. Give the 12-word spelling check.

questions.q: Spell 'measure.'
questions.a: m-e-a-s-u-r-e.

questions.q: How does a diagram help a how-to?
questions.a: It shows what to do in a picture.

weeks.assessment_key: How-to rubric (3 = proficient): introduction tells what you will make or do; materials list; numbered steps in correct order with time-order words; a closing; a reader can follow it without help. Spelling (suggested 12): ingredient, measure, sprinkle, minute, seedling, gather, together, important, number, finally, carefully, container.

weeks.prep: Gather stationery, an envelope, and a stamp; have a relative's mailing address ready. Write a sample friendly letter to label and 5 informal sentences to rewrite. Prepare two short science texts with comparison questions for Friday.
misconceptions: Forgetting commas in the greeting and closing. 'Dear Grandma,' and 'Love,' always end with a comma.
Using slang in formal speech. Practice 'Hey, what's up?' → 'Hello, how are you?'

days.guide: Compare talking to a friend vs. a museum guide. Rewrite 5 informal sentences formally.

questions.q: Make formal: 'Hey, can I see that rock?'
questions.a: Excuse me, may I please see that rock?

questions.q: When do we use formal language?
questions.a: With adults we don't know well, in letters to businesses, and in presentations.

days.guide: Learn the 5 friendly-letter parts and label a sample letter.

questions.q: Name the 5 parts of a friendly letter.
questions.a: Date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

questions.q: Punctuate the greeting: Dear Grandpa
questions.a: Dear Grandpa,

days.guide: Write a letter to a relative about 3 things learned about volcanoes, mountains, or earthquakes, using science words.

questions.q: Write a body sentence with a science word.
questions.a: Example: I learned that magma is melted rock under the ground.

questions.q: Where does the closing go?
questions.a: After the body, before the signature (e.g., 'Love,').

days.guide: Edit the letter, address the envelope with capitals for city and state, and mail it. Read a nonfiction passage and log it.

questions.q: Capitalize: sacramento, california
questions.a: Sacramento, California.

questions.q: Where does the return address go?
questions.a: The top left corner of the envelope.

days.guide: Give the unit test: compare two science texts, find the author's reasons, and check letter format.

questions.q: Fix: 'your friend' as a closing.
questions.a: Your friend,

questions.q: What does 'reasons support a point' mean?
questions.a: The author gives facts that show the point is true.

weeks.assessment_key: Letter format rubric (3 = proficient): date, greeting with comma, body with 3 science facts using science words, closing with comma, signature; envelope with capitalized city and state. Unit test: questions comparing the two texts answered with details from both; the author's point and reasons identified; letter-format items correct (comma after greeting and closing).

weeks.prep: Get Winnie-the-Pooh (A. A. Milne, public domain in the U.S.) and preview chapters 1–3. Set up a book-club journal (chapter, characters, what happened, favorite part, question).
misconceptions: Describing characters without evidence ('Pooh is silly'). Add 'because in the story he…'
Missing the humor. Stop and ask 'Why is this funny?' — often the characters misunderstand something.

days.guide: Read Chapter 1. Describe Pooh's plan to get honey and why it fails. Start a book-club journal page.

questions.q: What is Pooh's plan to get honey?
questions.a: He rolls in mud to look like a small black rain cloud and floats up to the bees' tree holding a balloon.

questions.q: Why does the plan fail?
questions.a: The bees are suspicious, so Christopher Robin has to shoot the balloon with his popgun to bring Pooh down.

days.guide: Read Chapter 2 (Pooh gets stuck at Rabbit's). Discuss how Pooh and Rabbit each respond. Read Pooh's lines in his voice.

questions.q: Why does Pooh get stuck in Rabbit's door?
questions.a: He ate too much honey and condensed milk and became too fat to fit through.

questions.q: How does Rabbit respond?
questions.a: He is annoyed but makes the best of it — he uses Pooh's back legs as a towel-horse.

days.guide: Make a character-trait web for Pooh, Piglet, Rabbit, Owl, and Eeyore with text examples.

questions.q: Give a trait for Eeyore with evidence.
questions.a: Gloomy — he is always sad and expects bad things.

questions.q: Give a trait for Piglet.
questions.a: Small and nervous (timid) — he worries during the Woozle hunt.

days.guide: Read Chapter 3 (the Woozle hunt) and explain the joke. Discuss with a family member, taking turns and asking questions.

questions.q: What is the joke in the Woozle chapter?
questions.a: Pooh and Piglet are following their own footprints around the trees, so the 'Woozles' are really them.

questions.q: Who figures it out?
questions.a: Christopher Robin (and then Pooh realizes).

days.guide: The child answers written who/what/why questions on chapters 1–3 and does a one-minute fluency read.

questions.q: Who is Christopher Robin?
questions.a: The boy who is friends with Pooh and helps the animals.

questions.q: Why does Pooh want to climb the tree in Chapter 1?
questions.a: He hears buzzing and wants honey.

weeks.assessment_key: Journal entries: one per chapter with characters, main event, and a question. Written comprehension (model): Ch. 1 — Pooh tries to get honey from the bees by floating up with a balloon while covered in mud to look like a little black rain cloud; it fails because the bees are suspicious, and Christopher Robin shoots the balloon to get him down. Ch. 2 — Pooh eats so much honey and condensed milk at Rabbit's house that he gets stuck in the doorway for a week until he is thin enough to be pulled out. Ch. 3 — Pooh and Piglet follow tracks around a spinney, but the tracks are their own. Fluency: record WCPM.

weeks.prep: Preview Winnie-the-Pooh chapters 4 and 6. Gather sticky notes, a story-structure chart (beginning/problem, middle, ending/solution), and a list of 30 irregular words (said, laugh, enough, friend, people, because, again, any, many, does, though, through, eye, four, …).
misconceptions: Thinking point of view means the narrator only. Ask how each character felt about the same event.
Sounding out irregular words letter by letter. Practice them as whole words by sight.

days.guide: Read Chapter 4 (Eeyore loses a tail). Discuss how the beginning introduces the problem and the ending solves it.

questions.q: Where is Eeyore's tail?
questions.a: Owl is using it as a bell-pull on his door.

questions.q: How is the problem solved?
questions.a: Pooh brings it back and Christopher Robin nails it back on Eeyore.

days.guide: Read Chapter 6 (Eeyore's birthday). Tell the gift story from Piglet's view, then Eeyore's.

questions.q: What happens to Pooh's gift?
questions.a: He eats the honey on the way, so he gives Eeyore the empty pot — a 'Useful Pot to Keep Things In.'

questions.q: What happens to Piglet's balloon, and how does Eeyore feel?
questions.a: Piglet falls and pops it; Eeyore is happy because the burst balloon fits in and out of the pot.

days.guide: Review 30 irregular words with a speed-read game and a spelling self-check.

questions.q: Spell 'friend' and 'because.'
questions.a: f-r-i-e-n-d; b-e-c-a-u-s-e.

questions.q: Which part of 'said' is irregular?
questions.a: The ai says short e.

days.guide: Perform a scene from Eeyore's birthday with voices for Pooh, Piglet, and Eeyore.

questions.q: How should Eeyore's voice sound?
questions.a: Slow, low, and gloomy.

questions.q: How should Piglet sound after popping the balloon?
questions.a: Worried and sorry.

days.guide: The child fills a story-structure chart for one chapter and writes a paragraph on how two characters felt differently about the same event.

questions.q: How did Pooh and Eeyore feel about the empty honey pot?
questions.a: Pooh felt a little embarrassed about eating the honey; Eeyore was delighted with a useful pot.

questions.q: What does a story ending do?
questions.a: Solves the problem and wraps up the story.

weeks.assessment_key: Story-structure chart (Chapter 4): Beginning — Eeyore has lost his tail; Middle — Pooh searches and visits Owl; Ending — Pooh sees Owl's bell-pull is Eeyore's tail, and Christopher Robin nails it back on. Point-of-view paragraph (Eeyore's birthday): Piglet feels upset and embarrassed that he popped the balloon; Eeyore is pleased because he can put the burst balloon in and out of his Useful Pot. Rubric 3 = both characters' feelings explained with evidence. Reader's theater: different voices, fluent reading.

weeks.prep: Preview Winnie-the-Pooh Chapter 10. Gather favorite books from the year and a computer or tablet for typing. Write 20 review spelling words from the year (said, friend, because, people, rain, beach, boat, night, bird, turn, happy, sky, unhappy, helpful, didn't, little, write, right, there, their).
misconceptions: Book reviews that retell the whole story, including the ending. Summarize the beginning only — no spoilers.
Reasons that are just opinions repeated. Each reason should point to something in the book.

days.guide: Read Chapter 10 (the party for Pooh). Discuss how the book ends. Rate the book with stars and give a reason.

questions.q: Why does Christopher Robin give a party?
questions.a: To honor Pooh for his clever idea to rescue Piglet during the flood.

questions.q: What gift does Pooh get?
questions.a: A special pencil case with pencils.

days.guide: Choose the favorite book of the year and plan a review: summary without spoilers, opinion, 3 reasons, recommendation.

questions.q: What is a spoiler?
questions.a: Telling the ending or a surprise.

questions.q: Give a recommendation sentence.
questions.a: Example: Kids who love funny animals will enjoy this book.

days.guide: Draft the review with linking words and at least 4 describing words.

questions.q: Give 2 describing words for Frog and Toad.
questions.a: Examples: funny, kind, cozy.

questions.q: Name linking words for reasons.
questions.a: because, also, another reason.

days.guide: Type the review with help, add a cover picture, and print or share it.

questions.q: Which key makes a capital letter?
questions.a: The Shift key.

questions.q: Why add a cover picture?
questions.a: So readers know which book it is.

days.guide: Read the review aloud and listen to a family member's; give the 20-word spelling test.

questions.q: Spell 'people.'
questions.a: p-e-o-p-l-e.

questions.q: Spell 'their' (belongs to them).
questions.a: t-h-e-i-r.

weeks.assessment_key: Book review rubric (3 = proficient): short summary without the ending; clear opinion; 3 reasons with examples; linking words; recommendation ('Readers who like… will enjoy this'). Cumulative spelling test of 20 words: 17+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Choose an on-level end-of-year fluency passage with 4–5 comprehension questions. Prepare the phonics/spelling inventory (vowel teams, r-controlled, prefixes/suffixes, two-syllable words, irregular words). Gather the year's writing portfolio and a summer reading list template.
misconceptions: Picking portfolio pieces by neatness only. Choose pieces that show growth and different kinds of writing.
Setting a vague summer goal ('read a lot'). Make it measurable: '10 books' or '20 minutes a day.'

days.guide: The child reads an on-level passage for one minute and answers comprehension questions. Compare with fall and mid-year scores.

questions.q: How do you find WCPM?
questions.a: Count words read in one minute and subtract errors.

questions.q: Why compare to fall?
questions.a: To see how much reading has grown.

days.guide: Give the phonics and spelling inventory and the irregular-word reading check.

questions.q: Spell 'unhappy.'
questions.a: u-n-h-a-p-p-y.

questions.q: Spell 'night.'
questions.a: n-i-g-h-t.

days.guide: Choose 5 best pieces (narrative, fable, report, opinion, poem) and write a one-sentence reflection for each.

questions.q: Write a reflection sentence for a fable.
questions.a: Example: My fable shows I learned to end a story with a clear lesson.

questions.q: Why include different kinds of writing?
questions.a: To show all the kinds of writing you learned.

days.guide: Present the portfolio to family, reading one favorite piece aloud and explaining one way you grew as a writer.

questions.q: Give an example of growth.
questions.a: Example: I now use temporal words and details in my stories.

questions.q: What makes a good presentation?
questions.a: Clear voice, eye contact, and answering questions.

days.guide: Make a summer reading list of 10 books and set a reading goal. Celebrate the year.

questions.q: Name a series to add to the list.
questions.a: Examples: Frog and Toad, Henry and Mudge, Magic Tree House.

questions.q: Write a measurable reading goal.
questions.a: Example: I will read 20 minutes every day this summer.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency: record WCPM and compare to fall and mid-year (end-of-grade-2 goal about 90–100 WCPM). Comprehension: 4/5 correct. Phonics inventory: record correct/incorrect for vowel teams (rain, play, tree, beach, boat, snow, night), r-controlled (car, corn, her, bird, turn), prefixes/suffixes (unhappy, reread, helpful, quickly), two-syllable words (paper, raincoat), and irregular words (said, friend, because, people). Portfolio: 5 pieces with one-sentence reflections; presentation explains one way the child grew.
